subsubtopic: TWENTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF TREMBLAY-BRASSARD COUPLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last night a big family party was held in Lafontaine Park to celebrate the 20th anniversary of the Tremblay-Brassard team. As reported by Jocelyne Lepage in today's La Presse, the family turned out in large numbers and brought together the whole Quebec theatre community.
Mr. Speaker, it must be said that the play Les belles-soeurs, first presented 20 years ago, in August 1968, marked a major turning point in the history of Quebec theatre. It was a decisive turning point, as actress Rita Lafontaine said, and she added, "We did not know it would become such a historic monument."
It is true, Mr. Speaker, that when Les belles-soeurs came out, many of us were shocked by the language. But since then, that play and all the plays by Tremblay and Brassard are part of our culture and our heritage.
So I say to them, "Congratulations and thanks!" Many of us will go to the Outremont Theatre on September 6 to see Le vrai monde.

subsubtopic: WESTERN GRAIN STABILIZATION PROGRAM-EXPANSION OF CROP COVERAGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, following final passage of amendments to the Western Grain Stabilization Program, I wish to recognize the successful efforts of the Minister of State for Grains and
Oilseeds (Mr. Mayer) and many members of our western caucus. The stabilization program changes will expand and improve the safety net for prairie farmers by adding nine new crops to the list of eligible crops, by authorizing a $750 million debt write-down, and by increasing the level of payments for rejoiners, new farmers and conditional participants.
Under the new legislation a producer joining the program will now receive a 70 per cent payment. Next year it will increase to 85 per cent. The stabilization program is an important source of income support for western producers. This Government has provided comprehensive, long-term support and leadership in this type of income program.
I want to recognize the efforts of all Members in acknowledging the hard work that this Government has put in on prairie agriculture and the fact that we have worked with and stood beside the farm families of western Canada in a time of need.

subsubtopic: CONDITIONS IN NORTHERN ONTARIO COMMUNITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I recently received a letter from the newly elected Grand Chief of the Nishnawbe Aski Nation, Mr. Bentley Cheechoo. This letter details some $11.4 billion in government expenditures proposed for the Defence Department. Grand Chief Cheechoo then points out that the 44 Nishnawbe-Aski communities across northern Ontario are forced to live in inadequate housing, with unhealthy water supplies and unsanitary sewage disposal. That is the situation for the "lucky" communities formally recognized by the Department of Indian Affairs.
For the six so-called new bands in the region, they cannot even get funding for schools, housing, or community infrastructure of any kind, which has led to scores of children receiving no schooling for the last two years.
To quote Grand Chief Cheechoo: "This is a national disgrace and the priorities of the federal Government should be realigned to demonstrate a caring and concern for those citizens in the greatest need ..." In the meantime, in spite of the Government's declared $40 million for family violence initiatives, four communities, three of which belong to Grand Council Treaty 3, have had funding for their highly successful crisis intervention programs summarily terminated.

August 24, 1988
Quoting Grand Chief Cheechoo again: "The best defence is a healthy, educated and informed population capable of handling international relations without the need to resort to war and weaponry".
The Government would be well advised to heed that advice.

subsubtopic: ARBITRATION AS DISPUTE SETTLING MECHANISM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the notion of arbitration is not a new concept for dispute settlement. Many societies, since the earliest of recorded times, have used this procedure as a quick and less costly dispute resolution mechanism. For example, the Hebrew Law of Judges required a judge to ask litigants at the outset of a trial whether they would submit to arbitration to settle their dispute.
Here in Canada arbitration has been recognized as a legitimate and significant part of our legal system. Every province and territory in Canada has an Arbitration Act, and the Parliament of Canada has approved legislation such as the Commercial Arbitration Act which permits the use of binding arbitration as a dispute settling mechanism.
I strongly urge the federal Government and those under federal jurisdiction to consider sourcing the Arbitrators Institute of Canada in all matters where a satisfactory resolution can be achieved through arbitration.

speechtext:

subsubtopic: FUNDING OF ABORIGINAL FRIENDSHIP CENTRES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a committee of the Canadian Bar Association has brought to the attention of all Canadians just how badly our justice system deals with aboriginal peoples. Extreme poverty, high unemployment, poor housing, and cultural conflict all combine to bring, in far too many cases, aboriginal people in urban settings into confrontation with the law. One of the few
August 24, 1988

agencies trying to prevent and respond to this crisis in the cities is the Aboriginal Friendship Centre.
These centres are doing a most commendable job under extremely difficult circumstances. The Government, however, is making their work even more difficult. Five months into this fiscal year, the Secretary of State (Mr. Bouchard) has yet to finalize their funding arrangements. subsubtopic: WHITEHORSE-INCLUSION OF FACILITIES IN NEW FEDERAL BUILDING URGED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Government has said it has a serious commitment to creating quality child care and claims to be making advances in that direction. In the Yukon this issue is very close to our hearts. We have a very young population. Not only do we have the second highest birth rate in Canada but we also have the highest percentage of working mothers.
There is a golden opportunity for the Government to demonstrate that it is willing to be innovative in creating solutions to the child care crisis. The new federal building being constructed in Whitehorse will house federal government offices as well as provide office space for private business. Employees have been unsuccessfully petitioning the Government to include child care space in that new building for well over a year. Numerous studies have shown that in the workplace child care facilities help to reduce employee absenteeism and generally improve the health and happiness of the employees and their children.
I strongly urge the Government to ensure that child care space is made available in this new federal building. It can only make the quality of life better for everyone.

subsubtopic: GROSSE ISLE, MAN.-SUPPORT FOR NEW RETAIL POSTAL OUTLET
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last night about 90 concerned residents of Grosse Isle, Manitoba, gathered in the community hall to discuss proposed changes to postal services in their community. The current postmaster is soon to leave the village.
The residents listened to Canada Post officials describe the options. They heard that they would be offered a retail postal outlet in their community. They heard that there would return all of the current postal services available to them. They heard that they would be able to choose postal lock boxes if they desired, that their addresses would not change, and that delivery would be the same as always. They heard that the new postal outlet would be open for a full 70 hours a week compared to the 21 hours it is now open.
They liked what they heard. With a unanimous show of hands, the residents of Gross Isle gave Canada Post Corporation the authority to implement a retail postal outlet prior to the end of the 90-day consultation period.
Gross Isle residents are joining the majority of rural Canadians who know that our Government has a commitment to improve postal service, and do not listen to the fears of NDP Members.

subsubtopic: CALL FOR FEDERAL PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a coalition of representatives from Canadian housing groups today visited the three political caucuses in Ottawa and outlined in startling terms how the federal Government is abdicating its federal responsibility for the provision of affordable housing for all Canadians.
Over 500,000 people across Canada do not have adequate housing. Over 100,000 people do not have any housing at all and are forced to live on the streets, in shelters, and in church basements.
The Government now provides 19,000 units of non-profit housing in all of Canada when estimates show that approximately 14,000 units are needed in the metropolitan area of Toronto alone. In the urban centres the Government is not releasing federal surplus lands to ease the pressure on housing and on the cost of land. There is no RHOSP-like program to encourage first-time home buyers among young married couples. There are no municipal incentives to encourage developments that facilitate progressive housing policies.
It is time that the federal Government picked up its federal responsibilities in the area of housing and delivered, because there is a social cost of not doing so.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I was here as well last night in my capacity as acting opposition whip for the next few weeks or so. I was in my chair at the time of the incident in question. It is true to say that with Parliament sitting long hours we sometimes all get a little hot under the collar and impatient. That probably happens not just to the Deputy Government House Leader (Mr. Lewis), as it obviously did, but to a number of us.
In defence of the position taken by the Deputy Speaker last night, it should be noted that no government Member had spoken for approximately an hour before. Obviously, the Deputy Speaker is quite in order to recognize whomever he wishes because, of course, it is his prerogative at any time.
Given the fact that no government Member had spoken for quite some time before that, he could have recognized another Member. It must also be appreciated by the Chair that in the cut and thrust of the activities at the time Members were rising on points of order and so on, which is distracting to the Chair at the best of times, as I am sure that you, Sir, will know.
The point that I am making, to assist the Chair, is that it could be said, of course, that the Deputy Government House Leader was upset with a ruling which was not in his favour. However, it would not be correct to say that the Deputy Speaker did not act properly by recognizing an Hon. Member from the Conservative Party because, of course, one had not been recognized for some time before that.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to point out that at the time that the question of the acceptability of a motion under Standing Order 9(4)(a) arose in the Chamber, I found myself in the awkward position of not being in my seat. I addressed some remarks to the Chair and to the Table, indicating that I had a great deal of difficulty understanding the difference between the words "consideration" and "completion".
The Chair will know that Standing Order 9(4)(a) uses the word "consideration", and I took the position that since there was a motion to put the question on the floor, the only interpretation that could be taken from the wording was that the words "completion" and "consideration" were the same. I submit and I have always felt that the essence of Standing Order 9(4) (a) is: "Do you have 15 Members to prevent completion of that stage?" That is the point that I was trying to make at the time.
I was making it informally and I was making it reasonably directly. I want to say that I took the precaution of checking Hansard to see if there was anything offensive recorded that I might wish, in the cool, hard light of the dawn, I had not said in the heat of the evening. In any event, if there was anything said by myself which was out of order, whether recorded in
Hansard or not recorded in Hansard, I would regret that very much and I would apologize to any person who took offence to what was said. There was certainly no offence intended, because we were well served by the Chair and by the Table. I have had previous correspondence over Standing Order 9(4)(a), and one of these days I will get it worded to the satisfaction of my impatience and perhaps the whole House.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MOTIONS TO CONTINUE SITTING ON BILL C-144
speechtext:
With great regard to the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary, I would intimate to him that I think the Chair has probably heard enough to deal with the matter. However, if it is very important, I will hear him. It does not always happen.
The matter that has been raised by the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) of course troubled me last night. As Hon. Members will know, our very excellent Deputy Speaker was in the chair. He is skilful, experienced and is an absolutely superb servant of this place. I know that all Hon. Members would agree with me on that. As is the obligation upon me, of course, I was here and when this matter was brought to my attention, I immediately came into the Chamber. There was no need for me to take the chair because the Deputy Speaker was completely in control of the House. I would point out it was with the co-operation of Hon. Members that he was completely in control of the House. However, I knew some Hon. Members were upset. I want Hon. Members to know that that concerns me, as I think it should. I was here for some minutes in the House during part of what has been alluded to. I was not in the chair, as I say. My hon. colleague was in the chair, but I was here.
I have reviewed the tapes very carefully. I might say to the Hon. Member for Regina East (Mr. de Jong), and I say this in a sympathetic way, that I listened most carefully this morning to the video tape of the Hon. Member's speech, and I say to him that I understand his feelings that were expressed last night. I say this because 1 think the Hon. Member should know that I understand those feelings.
The Hon. Member for Burnaby has raised a matter, and there are two parts to that matter. First, what happened here is that an Hon. Member from the government side rose on a motion. I will not go into the numbers, but I will try to simplify this for Hon. Members and for the public. Under the rules, within one hour of the time of adjournment an Hon. Member on either side can rise and move that the debate continue-if I can put it in colloquial terms-not that the debate be terminated or that it be completed. If there are 15 Members rising in opposition to that motion, that motion will not be accepted and the debate will end at the appointed hour, which was ten o'clock last night.
An Hon. Member from the government side rose and did not correctly put the motion. As I understand it, the Hon. Member did not carefully repeat the words of the Order and said that the matter be completed, which would mean, if one took those words seriously-and I am sure that it was an error on the part of the Hon. Member, and quite an innocent one- that all matters would have to be completed. That kind of
August 24, 1988

closure is not anticipated by the rules of time allocation or closure that we have.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MOTIONS TO CONTINUE SITTING ON BILL C-144
speechtext:
The Deputy House Leader, as the Hon. Member for Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme) is pointing out to me, and I always, as Hon. Members well know, defer with great respect to the Hon. Member for Saint-Denis because, quite frankly, he has been a great amount of strength to me as Speaker and he usually has something of good sense to say, not just to the House but also to the Speaker, and he correctly points out that the Deputy Speaker quite correctly rejected the motion that was put by the Member from the government side because it was incorrect. What followed then was that a number of Members rose to be recognized, including the Hon. Member for Regina East. I am instructed, because I inquired, that there had been seven opposition Members in a row speaking on debate. The Hon. Deputy Speaker, having rejected the motion that came from the government side, then went to the Government and recognized a Member on debate. I know that this has upset some Hon. Members and that is why I am referring to it.
1 have to ask Hon. Members to exercise some sympathy for the position of the Speaker. The Speaker is not supposed to be able to divine what will be in the mouth of the Hon. Member that he in fact recognized. The Hon. Member may very well have been rising to continue debate, and it is quite true that the Hon. Member for Regina East and I think others were on their feet. The difficulty the Speaker has is that one has to select someone. In this event, the Hon. Deputy Speaker, for whom everyone in the House has great respect, recognized a Member from the government side. This time, the Government got it right and put the motion to extend debate. It is not for me to say one way or the other as to why these things happen, but I suppose it is not altogether untoward for the Chair to comment that this time, the Government got it right and put the motion that the debate be continued.
First, we have a very strong tradition here that the Speaker does not overrule the Deputy Speaker. Under the circumstances, I think Hon. Members would agree with me that fault cannot be found with the Deputy Speaker. As it happened, debate did continue for a little while and then it concluded.
There is another matter, and that refers to what happened with the Deputy House Leader, as happens with Whips of all Parties and perhaps occasionally some other House Leaders. The responsibility of a House Leader is extraordinary at times, and the public should know this. This place does not function without responsible people in all three Parties working long, long hours to take responsibility for what their own Parties do and for the arrangements that are made intra-Party continually. We have been sitting a long time, and I am not getting into a discussion as to whether we should have or should not have. I am just saying that we have been sitting for a long time. The
Point of Order-Mr. Robinson
Hon. Minister of State has admitted that he made statements which the Hon. Member for Burnaby properly brought to the attention of the Chair and the House, statements which he admits he should not have made.
I do not think that I can take it any further except to say that most of the time, most of us, and some of you upon occasion recently have been assisting me, the Deputy Speaker and Acting Speakers, by taking the chair because we have had to call on some help, know that it is a great comfort to the Chair if Hon. Members will refrain from making comments except when they are in their places and they are recognized to be heard. The Hon. Member for Regina East can say that last night he was rising to be heard as were others, and sometimes when there is a lot of people up, it is very difficult for the Speaker to choose. I think the Hon. Minister of State has quite gallantly and quite properly expressed to the House his regret. The Hon. Member for Burnaby, I have to say, had every right to raise the matter and I thank him for the moderation with which he expressed it.

The Hon. Member for Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme) made some very interesting comments to the Chair, but he has preferred to remain silent.. . However, I see that may not be the case. The Hon. Member for Saint-Denis.

I would like to put this to you, and then I too will reflect on it, but I would not like to finish the day without putting it to you openly.
Perhaps in the future, the Government or any political Party might decide not to put up any speakers for a long time and therefore whoever is in the chair would recognize those who rise and would try to alternate between two of the three political Parties. I hope that I will not conclude, after what you said, that in the future, if such were to be the case again, if the Government or political Party would suddenly decide to put up speakers for debate, the Chair would decide that because the Government has not participated and that there were seven Members in a row from a political Party participating, the Chair would recognize six or seven Members of the Government in a row. That is a bit like what happened last night when two government Members in a row spoke because they had not participated for quite a while before. I would hope that we could try to clear that up, not today, but I would not like it to be a precedent because it could be a very dangerous precedent for future tactics for any of the three political Parties.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 106, I have the privilege to present a petition signed by a number of citizens from the Ottawa-Hull area who call upon Parliament to withdraw the Child Care Act forthwith because the Bill contains neither national objectives nor necessary funding arrangements, and will not ensure that
families have access to high quality child care. The child care Bill is not in the best interests of young children, women or families in Canada.

subsubtopic: IMMIGRATION-SPONSORING OF RELATIVES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is my honour and privilege to present three petitions under Standing Order 106 on different subjects. The first petition is signed by a number of residents of Toronto and concerns immigration. It refers to the need to allow unmarried sons and daughters of all ages to enter as family class and specifically points out that in 1986 the then Minister of Justice promised that the unfair distinction between Canadian citizens and permanent residents of three years or more would be eliminated so that both groups would have equal rights to sponsor parents of any age, and that this promise has not yet been fulfilled. The petitioners call upon this House to ensure that the Government will fulfil that promise.

subsubtopic: OPPOSITION TO BILL C-55
speechtext: My next petition is again signed by a number of residents of Toronto and other cities in Ontario. The petitioners point out that whereas Bill C-55 threatens Canada's traditional commitment to assisting refugees and sets out measures designed to keep most refugees out of the country as opposed to ensuring that genuine refugees are given protection, therefore, they humbly pray and call upon Parliament to ensure that the Government will withdraw Bill C-55 and substitute legislation embodying the principles of fair and quick oral hearings of claims of refugee claimants before a refugee board independent of the Immigration Commission, as well as universal access to such hearings for every applicant in Canada and the right to appeal on the basis of fact.

subsubtopic: CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my last petition is signed by a number of residents of Ontario who point out that the very fabric of Canadian sovereignty is threatened by the proposed Mulroney-Reagan trade deal which was not mandated in the last election and would reduce Canada's ability to plan the economic, social and cultural programs we need, and would integrate us further into the North American defence industrial base. The petitioners therefore urge that Parliament ensure that a national debate takes place on this Mulroney-Reagan trade deal before such an agreement is finalized.

subsubtopic: LABELLING OF FOOD INGREDIENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour and privilege to present a petition signed by some 40 residents of the communities of Winnipeg, Manitoba, Kenora, Dryden and Redditt, Ontario. This petition calls upon Parliament to enact legislation and regulations to ensure the thorough and comprehensive labelling of foods served in
August 24, 1988

restaurants and take-out shops in order to ensure that those who suffer from severe allergies, which indeed can be life threatening, have the information available to protect themselves.

subsubtopic: RESEARCH INTO PREVENTION AND CURE OF SCHIZOPHRENIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have two petitions to present this afternoon. The first petition is signed by residents of Thunder Bay. It concerns the very serious problem of the illness, schizophrenia, which affects about 1 per cent of the population causing severe mental anguish and suffering to the patients and their relatives and costing Canadian society more than $3 billion annually in direct health care and other support costs.
The petitioners note that recent research findings, including those obtained in Canada, show the illness to be a biochemical brain disorder in part caused by genetic malfunction. They are concerned that there is not enough research being done in Canada to determine what possibilities there are of treatment. Therefore, the petitioners call upon Parliament to ensure that research efforts related to schizophrenia will in future be commensurate with the very serious impact of this illness in Canada.

subsubtopic: CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my second petition is also signed by residents in northwestern Ontario and persons in Thunder Bay and outlying parts of the constituency of Thunder Bay-Nipigon. These are persons who note that the Conservative Government had no mandate from the Canadian people to conclude a free trade agreement with the United States. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) promised that in the course of the bilateral trade negotiations that Canadian sovereignty would not be compromised, but the petitioners assert that the trade agreement negotiated by the Mulroney Government threatens the very fabric of Canadian political and economic sovereignty by removing the power of the Canadian Government to effectively control foreign ownership, develop Canadian energy resources in the best interest of Canadians, and equalize opportunities between the regions.
Since Canada would be denied this policy freedom by the agreement, the petitioners call upon Parliament to dissolve and allow the people of Canada the opportunity to reject the proposed free trade agreement during a national general election.

subsubtopic: PARTICIPATION IN UNITED NATIONS IRAN-IRAQ MILITARY OBSERVERS GROUP
speechtext:
That this House supports Canadian participation in the United Nations Iran/Iraq Military Observers Group (UNIIMOG) to observe the ceasefire between Iran and Iraq and hopes that Canada's contribution to this international initiative will result in an end to hostilities and a lasting peace.
He said: Mr. Speaker, 10 days ago I stood with the Chief of Defence Staff on the tarmac of the Canadian Forces Base, Trenton, to wish Godspeed to the first of our troops who were leaving for Iran and Iraq as part of the United Nations force in that region. I wish every Canadian could have been with us. The range of emotions present at that time is not surprising.

August 24, 1988
Peacekeeping
There was pride because Canada was trying to help to end a war that has cost a million lives. There was sadness at leaving families and friends behind for a foreign tour of duty which could last up to six months or longer. There was apprehension because Canadians know from bitter experience that trying to keep the peace could be hazardous. There was enthusiasm because all of the soldier's training was suddenly made relevant at that moment. And there was hope because it appeared that peace, although far from certain, was now more possible than ever before in a bloody eight-year conflict.
No one should underestimate the sacrifices these troops and their families have been asked to make. Some of them have had to postpone weddings or interrupt honeymoons as the soldiers do their duty outside of Canada. Others will have children born while they are away or will have family crises arise and they will not be able to be there to attend to them. For their families, the burden of a lengthy separation will be compounded by a concern for the safety of the troops. For each of these soldiers, these were sacrifices they were prepared to make to serve Canada and to promote peace. As they take on their heavy new responsibilities, the hopes and prayers of every Canadian go with them.
I have placed this motion before the Flouse today, not to fulfil a legal obligation but because I believe that when such a major new undertaking is given, I have a moral responsibility to report to the peoples' representatives to ask for their support. With your permission, Mr. Speaker, and with the consent of our colleagues, I would like to table in both official languages, the Orders in Council authorizing our troops to be sent in support of the United Nations Forces. If there would be unanimous consent, perhaps I could table those Orders in Council at this time.

subsubtopic: PARTICIPATION IN UNITED NATIONS IRAN-IRAQ MILITARY OBSERVERS GROUP
speechtext:
Agreed.
What is at issue here? Why did Canada agree to send troops on this mission? Let me, first, report on how events have developed.
On July 21, an informal approach was made to Canada by the Secretary General of the United Nations, Perez de Cuellar. He wanted to determine our willingness to participate in a peacekeeping operation, if it was possible to negotiate a cease- fire. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) and I responded that, if Canada were approached formally, we hoped that a positive response could be made.
On August 9, during the recent parliamentary recess, following the most commendable and successful efforts of the Secretary General, we were indeed approached formally. The Secretary of State for External Affairs and I responded on behalf of the Government that, in keeping with Canada's long established traditions, we would participate in the United Nations Iran-Iraq Military Observer Group, or UNIIMOG, and provide, on a temporary basis, sufficient military signals personnel to satisfy the total requirement of the United
Nations force. These signals experts will take up the total signals responsibilities along a 1,200 kilometre frontier. It is a heavy responsibility, but it is one that will be done exceptionally well.
Last Saturday the Iranian and Iraqi armed forces implemented a cease-fire ending eight years of bloody fighting between those two countries. Great losses were sustained, not only among the opposing forces, but also among the civilian population. Our best estimate is that over one million people have been killed in what must surely have been one of the longest and bloodiest conflicts of this century. In the course of this war, peaceful navigation and trade were disrupted in the Persian Gulf, leading to the intervention of western naval forces. This, in turn, gave rise to fears of a possible superpower conflict. Now finally an opportunity exists to resolve this conflict by peaceful means.
Between those two hostile armies, in what was only recently a battlefield, the unarmed United Nations observers will interpose themselves and monitor the pullback operations and the cease-fire. Negotiation of a comprehensive settlement of the underlying issues in the conflict will begin in Geneva tomorrow.
In response to the United Nations request we immediately selected 15 Canadian Forces officers to join a total observation force of 330 from 24 countries, including NATO, Warsaw Pact, neutral, and non-aligned states. The Security Council approved the mandate of the observer group for a six-month period with the option of renewal. If observers are still required beyond that time, a further request would have to be made to the participating countries.
Because of Canada's recognized experience and expertise in supplying communications support to peacekeeping operations, we have sent 500 officers and men, in addition to our 15 observers, to take up positions in both Iran and Iraq. The United Nations has committed itself to replacing our signallers and their equipment with United Nations civilians as soon as an appropriate force can be raised and trained. We expect that the civilianization of the communications elements can be accomplished well within the next year. We will press for the replacement of these troops, who form by far the largest portion of our contingent, at the earliest possible moment, so that they can return to their regular duties.
I am proud to tell the House that our contingent includes Reservists who will be working alongside the regular force members. Indeed, it is the first time that Reservists have been sent into a peacekeeping operation as part of the first wave. The House will know that last year I authorized the posting of an additional 60 Reservists to our peacekeeping forces in Cyprus, and they have acquitted themselves exceptionally well in this theatre. Our increasing use of Reservists in the mainstream activities of the Canadian Forces underscores the vital role they play, and demonstrates that the total force concept, which will give us a fully-integrated military, is proceeding well.
August 24, 1988

We recognize that this deployment entails risks for members of the Canadian Forces. We have carefully weighed those risks. Our soldiers who have accepted this challenge understand the danger. We believe, as do our military authorities, that they are acceptable in light of what is at stake. As I have already stated, the cease-fire is holding. Should hostilities recommence, however, our troops will be withdrawn at the earliest opportunity.

According to United Nations guidelines, officers acting as observers are unarmed. However, for the purposes of selfprotection, the signals experts are provided with the new Canadian rifle. To avoid hazardous situations, such as land mines, our troops will take the usual precautions and, as far as possible, travel only on the main roads. When they do not, they will be guided by a vehicle from the host country. As a rule, the Canadian signals experts will be posted behind the front lines, and only officers acting as observers will patrol the front. The host countries will provide liaison officers and will look after the safety of our troops.

I want to turn to an issue that often arises when we undertake peacekeeping activities. The Department of National Defence is proud of its policy against discrimination on the basis of religious beliefs, colour, creed, and sex. This has been clearly demonstrated by the Government's policy toward women in the Canadian forces. Since I have been Minister, I have expanded employment opportunities for women both in the variety of occupations and in the type of units in which they may work.

subsubtopic: PARTICIPATION IN UNITED NATIONS IRAN-IRAQ MILITARY OBSERVERS GROUP
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: PARTICIPATION IN UNITED NATIONS IRAN-IRAQ MILITARY OBSERVERS GROUP
speechtext:
At this time we have female Canadian Armed Forces members serving in the Sinai in Cyprus. However, we face a difficult choice when agreeing to participate in a peacekeeping operation such as the one in Iran and Iraq. The acceptability of Canada, together with the 23 other nations, to the peacekeeping mission is contingent upon being seen as completely impartial, and as being seen as not in contradiction with local customs.
United Nations practice is to respect the traditions, customs, and religious practices and beliefs of host countries where United Nations peacekeeping forces are deployed.
The U.N. expects countries participating in its operations to respect this position. While we will abide by United Nations practice, we will also make it clear that Canadian policy is to ensure that our Canadian Armed Forces reflect the social fabric of Canada. The goal of Canadian observers is to assist in any way possible to end the senseless killing and to help to promote peace. Our choice in this case is very simple. It is either to respect the host country's views regarding the makeup of the peacekeeping forces or refuse to participate and allow the killing to continue. I stressed this fact when the United Nations first approached us, particularly with regard
Peacekeeping
to our signals experts. The United Nations said that Canada was the only country it knew of capable of fulfilling this function. Had we not been prepared to send our troops we might very well have seen hostilities continue. We believe that, if we can help to end a war that has taken a million lives, that must be our priority.
I want to mention another issue that is of great importance to us. You will recall that the Department of National Defence has recently been criticized for its work to improve devices used by our forces to protect themselves against chemical and biological warfare. That work is strictly defensive in nature, and we continue to press for a complete ban world-wide on chemical and biological weapons. But, until that day arrives, sending Canadian peacekeepers into an area where chemical agents have been used underscores the need for the Canadian Forces to be prepared to work in a chemical warfare environment and, in particular, it underscores the need for our research establishments to develop even more effective devices to protect our personnel.
Putting this in the simplest possible terms, if we did not have adequate training for our Canadian Forces personnel, and if we did not have adequate equipment of a defensive nature for our Canadian Forces personnel, we would not have been able to deploy our troops to this region where chemical agents have been used. It would not further the cause of peace to have us unable to send Canadian troops to this region. That is why this work is so important for Canada. I can report to the House that we have issued chemical detection devices, gas masks, and protective clothing to our troops.

As announced, the deployment of our forces was without incident. Occasionally deployment in the border zone raised some problems, for instance with respect to the carrying of weapons, and all military peace-keeping personnel were required to carry passports issued by their country of origin. These problems have now been dealt with, and we expect our peace-keeping forces will soon be in place throughout the region. Between now and August 28, we expect all our troops to be at their post, as planned.

Let me underscore this fact for the House. We expect that in any case where peacekeeping troops are being asked to move into a region on very short notice there will obviously be transitional difficulties. I am informed by the Chief of the Defence Staff that our ability to get our troops and equipment in place and operating effectively has been as good in this instance as ever before in any Canadian peacekeeping operation that we have participated in. It is a credit to the Canadian troops and to all of those in the United Nations and to the host countries, that such success has been realized.
Our target of our troops in place and operational is August 28. We expect that our troops will be in place and that the vast

August 24, 1988
Peacekeeping
bulk of our equipment will be there and functioning at that time.
I might also indicate that while there have been problems- and I have indicated that earlier-we expected that there would be problems from time to time as such an operation took place.
We see a willingness on the part of both Iran and Iraq to see the cease-fire work. We have received co-operation from both sides, which has facilitated our work, and we are grateful for that.

Mr. Speaker, those were the salient points. As such, they do not give us a very accurate picture of the magnitude and importance of the enterprise in which we have become engaged.

Why is it important that Canadian troops participate? Why do we send Canadians abroad for extended periods to serve in situations which clearly entail some risk? In the White Paper which I tabled in this House a little over a year ago, I pointed out that regional instability and conflict have caused enormous human suffering and posed serious risks to the world community.
What better example could we find in the conflict that is raised between Iran and Iraq for over eight years at a cost of more than a million dead?
Could we ever find a better example of a conflict crying out for peacekeeping and resolving disputes by peaceful means?
There are, I know, those who do not share this view. Iran and Iraq have been dismissed as "lunatic countries" and it has been suggested that we should be staying at home, safe and sound, far from danger. I do not share that view and I believe that neither this House nor the Canadian people as a whole would have us shrink from a challenge so worth accepting. We in Canada are not among those who would write off peoples and nations less favoured than ourselves.
The House will recall that White Paper identified the peaceful settlement of disputes as one of the three pillars of Canadian security policy. We described peacekeeping as the vehicle by which the Canadian Forces contribute to that objective. It is an area in which Canada is uniquely positioned to make a contribution. We are not a superpower, but we operate sophisticated military equipment and our forces are highly professional. We are not a colonial power and are, therefore, acceptable throughout the world. We have no vested interest. Our goal is simply to save lives and end human suffering.
This Government is intent on rebuilding the Canadians Forces. We are resolved, and it bears repeating here today, to increase our contribution to peacekeeping.
Last October, for example, we increased our contingent in Cyprus to offset the withdrawal of Swedish troops. More recently, we agreed to take part in the Observer Group in Afghanistan and Pakistan and increased the personnel assigned to the Multinational Force and Observers in the Sinai. With the commitment which we are discussing today, we are at a high-water mark in the history of Canadian peacekeeping. Only once before, in Korea, did we do more.
These efforts in UN peacekeeping are in addition to a wide range of Canadian Forces humanitarian activities which take us throughout the world. Whether it is delivering school supplies, clothing or food aid, in the Caribbean or elsewhere, or the airlift that is currently under way by Canadian Forces Hercules aircraft in Ethiopia, the Canadian Forces have dedicated their equipment and skills and training in their efforts to eliminate human suffering. It is a contribution for which all Canadians should be tremendously proud.

subsubtopic: PARTICIPATION IN UNITED NATIONS IRAN-IRAQ MILITARY OBSERVERS GROUP
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: PARTICIPATION IN UNITED NATIONS IRAN-IRAQ MILITARY OBSERVERS GROUP
speechtext:
Moving over 500 men, their vehicles and other related equipment across the world into what was only recently a battlefield is certainly no easy task. It is being carried out with the skill and professionalism that we take for granted in the Canadian Forces. We can but admire the way this operation has been conducted.
I am confident that the members of the Canadian Forces that we have committed to this endeavour will acquit themselves with credit, as they have done so often before in other peacekeeping operations. I am also certain that they will contribute greatly to the peace process which began in Iran and Iraq with the cease-fire of August 20.
As I mentioned earlier, there is another important group that is also making sacrifices for the success of this mission. I refer, of course, to the families and loved ones of our peacekeepers. I know that sacrifices have already been made and many more will be made by service families. To them I promise three things: first, we will do everything that we can to ensure the safety of the troops. Second, we will work to bring them home as soon as possible, and, third, we will do everything that we can to assist the families of those serving abroad.
I have asked the Chief of the Defence Staff to join us today, both to represent the determination of all of the members of the Canadian Forces to see this mission through and also so that he can relay to our troops the wholehearted support and the best wishes of the House as they meet that challenge.
There is no higher calling that any soldier can receive than to be asked to promote peace and to end the suffering of those who have suffered for far too long. Our troops have answered the call, and Canadians stand united in offering them our admiration and respect in sending them our prayers for a safe return from a successful mission.

subsubtopic: PARTICIPATION IN UNITED NATIONS IRAN-IRAQ MILITARY OBSERVERS GROUP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we in the
Official Opposition support the Canadian participation in this
August 24, 1988

fine initiative on the part of the United Nations. Reaching back to former Prime Minister Lester Pearson, we find ample evidence that Canadians believe in the United Nations, support initiatives in the defence of peace and are proud of Canada's involvement.
We welcome also the efforts and the continuation of Canada's effort in pressing hard for a ban on chemical warfare, a front on which Canada has been active for several decades.
In the case of the Iran-Iraq mission, our Canadian contingent consists of 498 individuals, including 370 communications personnel, 113 support personnel and 15 observers who will serve on the front. Considering the fact that the United Nations mission is of 850 people, drawn from 24 nations, Canada's contribution represents almost two-thirds of the total force.
This is Canada's sixteenth participation in a United Nations peacekeeping mission, and the task is to patrol a frontier 1,200 kilometres long and to observe that the two parties maintain the cease-fire agreed upon on August 8.
The Minister made reference to the one million casualties on both sides, and he also made reference to the disruption in the movement of ships and air traffic in the Persian Gulf. We regret, on this side of the House, that he made no reference to the recent and very tragic event of the U.S. navy shooting down a civilian passenger plane carrying the Iranian flag, which somehow represented a turning point for international global outrage as to what was happening in this area, and perhaps it was significant in bringing about the negotiations at the United Nations.
If we look to the past, we see that over the past 39 years Canada has participated in 15 peacekeeping missions involving 77,000 military personnel. Over the past 39 years, Canadian personnel went to Kashmir, Korea, Jerusalem, Lebanon, Zaire, New Guinea, Yemen, India, Pakistan, Egypt, the Dominican Republic, Cyprus, the Golan Heights and Afghanistan.
It is important to remember that in the performance of our international peacekeeping duty 78 Canadians have lost their lives and, in addition to that, 312 died in Korea. That represents our contribution until now. As to the future, it is anticipated that as many as 1,000 Canadian troops may be requested next year to oversee the cease-fire in Namibia. Other requests may follow, possibly to serve in Nicaragua, Kampuchea and in the western Sahara.
The Minister made a reference to the White Paper which, if looked at close range, merely affirms Canada's current commitment to international peacekeeping. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Beatty) proposes that future peacekeeping requests be judged on a case by case basis. While doing that he confirms the mechanics of peacekeeping but does not address the policy of peacekeeping. The White Paper, in
Peacekeeping
other words, fails to recognize the need for developing a more coherent and effective framework for United Nations intervention in regional conflicts so that peacekeeping forces are utilized effectively but not as an indefinite substitute to negotiated peace.
It is interesting to note as an over-all assessment to the White Paper what Professor Keating of the University of Alberta wrote through his following observation:
The Conservative Government's White Paper is guided by a cold war image of the Soviet threat, a concentration on the instruments of warfare and a rather benign view of American military interests in the Arctic.
What is the Liberal approach? We believe that peacekeeping must be discussed in relation to peacemaking. Canada in this process, of course, could play a pivotal role as a founding member of the United Nations and a leading force behind the creation of the peacekeeping idea. From the very beginning and under the constant and passionate leadership of Canadians in our foreign service and subsequently that of former Prime Minister Lester Pearson, Canada has a special responsibility to reflect on this role and how it could be improved. A Liberal Government would play an active role in encouraging the United Nations to review its peacekeeping strategies with the objective of making them more effective, aware of the change also in the position taken recently by the Soviet Union which is now actively willing to support United Nations peacekeeping activities for the first time.
The Liberal Party has called for Canada to seek re-election to a seat on the Security Council in part as a means to facilitate this initiative. In addition, a Liberal Government will review its own peacekeeping policies in order to give them a better framework of principles and goals which are sensitive to current and emerging trends in regional conflict and the possibilities for resolving them.
Some 20 years ago in his book Peace in the Family of Man former Prime Minister Pearson concluded in a manner still relevant today:
We must apply the science and art of politics to the affairs of the international community with the intensity of personal involvement that we give to domestic affairs.
That is an interesting linkage. He continued:
In the past, conflicts have led to wars within national boundaries. But normally we don't go to war over such disputes. If we do, we call it civil war. We must reach the point where we consider war between countries as civil war.
I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that Mr. Pearson was right then as he is right today because we are just beginning to consider war between two countries as a form of civil war affecting the global community, the entire international community.
This debate, which we welcome today, would be incomplete without looking at the United Nations in perspective. The late John Holmes, the former Under Secretary for External Affairs, in his lucid and incisive analysis of the United Nations entitled The United Nations in Perspective and published in

August 24, 1988
Peacekeeping
the series Behind the Headlines wrote the following interesting thoughts:
A new United Nations, if we could possibly build one, could not be very different in shape from the present one. In the meantime, however, the alternative would be anarchy, the naked clash of national wills, without institutions or rules in place to avert conflict. That was the situation that the great Hague peace conferences at the beginning of the century were intended to correct. The efforts at The Hague came too late to prevent the disaster of 1914, but the lesson was learned.
Out of the First World War came the First try. Although the League was regarded as a failure, it was taken for granted throughout the Second World War that we would try again. The second effort is broader and deeper and has already lasted twice as long. There is no fast track to peace; it requires constant vigilance and invention.
In conclusion, we in the Liberal Party support Canadian participation in the United Nations Iran-Iraq Military Observers Group to observe the ceasefire between Iran and Iraq and hope that Canada's contribution to this international initiative will result in an end to hostilities and a lasting peace. This motion is consistent with the tradition and the history of the Liberal Party of Canada.
We wish our military group well and we hope that their mission will be crowned with success.

subsubtopic: PARTICIPATION IN UNITED NATIONS IRAN-IRAQ MILITARY OBSERVERS GROUP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to participate in this debate with rather mixed emotions. On the one hand I and my Party are totally in agreement with the move the Government has made with respect to sending peacekeepers to that war-torn area of the world, Iran and Iraq. We support the Government's initiative and we also send our best wishes for a safe and speedy return to the Canadian soldiers serving there. We know they will acquit themselves with both confidence and distinction, but that goes without saying. That is the motherhood aspect of this motion today.
What confuses me or makes me somewhat angry is that we are here today debating a motion with which all three Parties are in agreement. There is no need really for a vote later on today and probably there will not be one when this same Government-I am not directing my anger at the Minister in this case but at the Government itself-closed down debate on the free trade Bill yesterday at report stage by using closure. It has on its plate right now the child care Bill, the broadcasting Bill and tax reform, all very major, contentious issues. All we hear on radio and television and read in the media these days is that the Opposition is somehow dragging out this session and preventing the Government from getting on with its legislative timetable. Yet, here this afternoon, the Government has seen fit to spend several hours, or what was supposed to have been several hours had we gotten started at three o'clock, debating this issue that is not contentious.
I think quite strongly that there is a deep reason for debating this matter this afternoon and that is to deflect public attention away from the very contentious issues in the Government's White Paper, the cold war rhetoric contained in it which relates more to the early 1950s than the to the 1980s
and 1990s, and instead bring on a new, refreshing emphasis on the peace aspects of defence.
I agree with the Minister and with the spokesperson for the Liberal Party that Canada has indeed an enviable record in peacekeeping. I also want to stress that the New Democratic Party and its predecessor, the CCF, were very staunch supporters of peacekeeping long, long before Suez, going back to the late 1940s and the early 1950s. That is another reason why we do not quarrel at all with this initiative on the part of the Government.
We know that it would have been a terrible waste had we decided not to send our troops to the Iran-Iraq area, considering how well trained they are, considering the fact that they are experts in communications, and considering the fact that Canadian troops and Canada are highly regarded throughout the world. I will not say it is refreshing, because no one really likes the idea of sending troops to a potentially dangerous area of the world, although we know it is a duty and a responsibility to do so, but I think it is particularly gratifying that Canada was called upon and that Canada has responded in a positive fashion. Had we not, we would have been letting down not only ourselves but, more important, the United Nations.
It is nice to see a revitalization, and I hope it is a genuine one, in respect for the United Nations, respect which has been sadly lacking for the last 10 or 15 years during which superpower politics have dominated the world stage. Here is a golden opportunity for middle powers such as Canada, with the United Nations, to re-enter the international field and to declare to the world that the future of mankind does not and should not depend on decisions taken in Moscow and Washington alone but that we are all members of the world community and we all have a contribution to make toward world peace and keeping world peace.
I mentioned a moment ago that I suspect very strongly that the real impetus behind debating this motion today was to deflect public opinion away from the more controversial aspect of the government White Paper. For a long time now, the nuclear-powered submarine program has been at the forefront of criticism. There are those who are very strongly for it, such as government Members, and there are those who are very strongly opposed to it, such as members of the two opposition Parties, and there is also a split in the academic community and in the general community.
I have another regret. Today we are discussing a motherhood issue dealing with the Canadian military and its capabilities, but we have never had an opportunity to debate fully in the House the government White Paper. That White Paper was introduced some 14 months ago and we have yet to have a full-fledged debate on a Canadian defence policy. I think that is regrettable. I suspect one of the reasons we have not debated it is that, in addition to the nuclear-powered submarine issue, there is another major issue in the White Paper, namely, the total force concept or total force approach to increasing and expanding the Canadian Armed Forces.
August 24, 1988

Very few people in Canada fully appreciate that according to some experts who have done some arithmetic, it would cost the Canadian taxpayers, to complete that total force concept and put it into practice, not $8 billion as the Government alleges the nuclear-powered submarines will cost, but $27 billion over 15 years. I would hope that the Minister would someday give us an opportunity to debate in full the government White Paper so that the people of Canada will have an opportunity to know what the three Parties think about that White Paper.
The motion before us reads:
That this House supports Canadian participation in the United Nations Iran/Iraq Military Observers Group (UNIIMOG) to observe the ceasefire between Iran and Iraq and hopes that Canada's contribution to this international initiative will result in an end to hostilities and a lasting peace.
I have already risen in the House briefly to put on the record my Party's thoughts on this issue, so today we are just a little bit late in debating the peacekeeping force. I want to reiterate right now what I said the other day to put in context my remarks of this afternoon. A few days ago, I said:
Mr. Speaker, this party has always been a strong advocate of the United Nations and its peacekeeping role. That's why I'm very happy that Canada is taking part in the peacekeeping force that's on its way to the Persian Gulf. And I'd like to offer my party's official support for this action. We can only enhance Canada's international reputation as a peaceful nation by helping to supervise the ceasefire between Iran and Iraq. We all hope this will also contribute to the final resolution of this conflict. It might even show other troubled nations that there is a way to resolve their differences peacefully. And it will surely strengthen the role of the United Nations in resolving international disputes.
I wish our troops well. May they have a safe trip and, more importantly, a speedy return. Of course, that depends on Iran and Iraq. They must show the world that they are willing to resolve their differences peacefully. A ceasefire is better than war. But it's not enough. The world needs a lasting peace in this troubled region.
There is no doubt, as far as the New Democratic Party is concerned, that the move made by the Minister and the Government is completely acceptable to us. I suppose I could add one proviso, and that is that I sincerely hope that our presence there will not, if it is extended too long, become a part of the problem rather than the resolution of the problem. That is always a danger involved in peacekeeping, although I am not blaming anyone at this point.
For example, I firmly believe that we should remain in Cyprus. It is an extremely volatile island. I do not know if they will ever resolve their problems, quite frankly. However, it would appear that our presence there along with that of the other U.N. units has, over the years, become part of the problem. We have been responsible, unwittingly, for extending the problem without really having an opportunity to put pressure on the two sides to come to a resolution. As long as we are there, the two sides in Cyprus can say: "Well, at least we are safe, we are not shooting at each other, so let us continue, disunited, and at each other's throats figuratively speaking".
I might add that I was the only representative of the three Parties in the House to make the statement that I just quoted that day. One wonders why, if the Government thought the
Peacekeeping
matter was so important, we did not have this debate two weeks ago when the peacekeeping force was being put into place.
We should also consider what happened yesterday in the House, and I have already alluded to that. The Government just rammed its omnibus trade Bill through report stage. In fact, it used time allocation, commonly referred to as closure, to limit debate. It plans to give us just two more days to speak on the most controversial issue facing Canadians. By the Prime Minister's own admission, it is the most important single piece of legislation ever to come before any Canadian Parliament. The Government says it cannot afford to give us any more time. Yet it has a whole day to devote to this motion. One has to ask why, although I think in my opening remarks I addressed that issue, or at least gave my opinion on it. I also mentioned child care and other Bills such as the Broadcasting Act and so on which are being held up and which I think deserve immediate attention.
For days in advance everyone knew Canada was going to participate in the Iran-Iraq peacekeeping force. It was on every news broadcast and in every newspaper in the country. Yet the Minister had to schedule a big press conference to get his face on television. In fact, he interrupted his vacation to fly back and get in on the act. He even arranged to fly the press corps to Petawawa to get the right visual backdrop for the TV cameras. However, he did not count on the weather. That cancelled his flying circus. Instead of just releasing the details, he rescheduled the whole event in Ottawa and kept his officials and the media waiting until he arrived. Then he told everyone what they already knew: Mission accomplished. It sounds like a Keystone Cops farce but it shows how desperate the Government is becoming.

subsubtopic: PARTICIPATION IN UNITED NATIONS IRAN-IRAQ MILITARY OBSERVERS GROUP
speechtext: Do you never take the high road?

subsubtopic: PARTICIPATION IN UNITED NATIONS IRAN-IRAQ MILITARY OBSERVERS GROUP
speechtext: As politicians in this House we like to get on television as much as anyone.

subsubtopic: PARTICIPATION IN UNITED NATIONS IRAN-IRAQ MILITARY OBSERVERS GROUP
speechtext: We are looking at the farce right now standing up in the House.

subsubtopic: PARTICIPATION IN UNITED NATIONS IRAN-IRAQ MILITARY OBSERVERS GROUP
speechtext: On an issue like this could it not have been left up to the military to handle the public relations?

subsubtopic: PARTICIPATION IN UNITED NATIONS IRAN-IRAQ MILITARY OBSERVERS GROUP
speechtext: You are a joke.

subsubtopic: PARTICIPATION IN UNITED NATIONS IRAN-IRAQ MILITARY OBSERVERS GROUP
speechtext:
Would it not have been acceptable to the people of Canada to have senior military personnel make the announcement and officially wish the troops good luck and Godspeed without making a big television extravaganza out of the whole thing?
The Government is desperate to get out of the hole it dug
with its White Paper on national defence. Canadians were
embarrassed by the White Paper's cold war rhetoric and

August 24, 1988
Peacekeeping
expensive schemes like the nuclear powered submarine program. It looks as though the subs have been put on the back-burner, at least for the time being, and maybe forever. We do not know. However, I want to take this opportunity to underline the Government's philosophy and show how far out of touch it is with the reality of the thinking in this country today.
The Conservative White Paper said "Canadian security policy must respond to an international environment dominated by the rivalry between East and West. These two groups of nations, each led by a superpower, are in conflict". It went on from there, but I will not quote at length. The Conservatives are still locked in the cold war. Meanwhile, Canadians have left the Conservatives behind in their thinking. They realize the world is constantly changing. For instance, a poll just released the other day shows that most Canadians see the conflict between the superpowers as the greatest threat to their security. The Conservative philosophy does not fit.
Neither does the Conservative cold war have any relevance to peacekeeping. I am tempted to ask: Which side of the cold war are we on in Iran and Iraq? The fact is that Canadians do not want their Government to choose sides and heighten international conflict. They want Canada to be the honest broker working for international peace. That clearly is not a priority with the Government. In fact, if you look at the Government's White Paper you will see that the Conservatives devoted just four paragraphs out of an 89-page document to peacekeeping. That shows you that support for the UN and peacekeeping really is not important to the Government, at least not at the time the White Paper was put together.
Canadians have rejected the Conservative cold war vision of the world, and the Minister knows it. Now he is on his own little media campaign to try to tie his Government's image to peacekeeping. Otherwise, why are we not debating the submarine program here in the House? Why are we not debating the total force structure program here in the House? Both of those issues are contentious. I am not saying the programs are totally wrong. I am not saying they are totally right. I am asking why we are not having a Commons debate so Members can stand up and express their views on these very contentious aspects of the Government's White Paper? Canadians are not going to buy this kind of smoke-screen. They know what the Government believes and this little debate is not going to change their minds.
I would like to point out that my Party has been consistent in its support for peacekeeping and the UN. I would like to contrast our position with that of the Conservative Party by quoting from our policy document Canada's Stake in Common Security. It reads: "Canada's primary responsibility in its own defence is to contribute to the development of a just international order. The role of the United Nations is central to this process".
It is in that spirit that I am proud to repeat my Party's support for Canada's participation in the observer force being
set up between Iran and Iraq. I would like to see this country doing more of this kind of operation. In fact, I have called for Canada to have forces which might be better structured to respond to international calls for assistance. Some people do not like that idea, but I think Canada's participation in this force shows there is an important role for it to play. There is a need for a highly mobile force which can quickly deploy to trouble spots around the world. It helps the cause of peace. It also strengthens the role of the United Nations. I firmly believe that if the world is ever going to pull back from the brink of destruction it will take a concerted international effort. That is a multinational effort, not just a superpower effort. The mechanism to co-ordinate this effort should be the UN.
I might add that all member nations of the UN, including Canada, are going to have to push for this development. They are going to have to get away from the bi-polar cold war mentality that the Government's White Paper exemplifies. Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to support the motion now before the House. First of all, I would like to expand on what was said by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Beatty) regarding my Government's desire to unreservedly support this peace keeping mission, namely that this exercise is in line with the many recommendations contained in the White Paper on Defence published in 1987.
Mr. Speaker, according to the White Paper, we feel that the deployment of our armed forces under the auspices of the United Nations or other international organizations, for the purpose of peacekeeping or cease-fire surveillance, serves our own national interests as well as those of the world as a whole. I am sure that my colleagues share this view. That is why on October 1987, we agreed to reinforce our contingent in Cyprus to compensate for the withdrawal of Swedish troops. For the same reason we more recently agreed to join the group of military observers in Afghanistan and Pakistan. And for that very same reason, we did not hesitate to accede to the request of the Secretary General of the United Nations that we participate in the UN Iran-Iraq operation.
We are certainly not rushing blindly into this undertaking. In fact, every operation is considered very objectively. Before the Government agrees to participate, it must establish that the operation is in line with the policies set forth in the White Paper. In this case as in others, the Government made its decision after considering to what extent the Iran-Iraq situation met the following criteria:
First of all, is there a clear and feasible mandate? It is obvious that the two warring factions agreed with the Secretary General on the UN's mandate, which is to supervise the cease-fire so that negotiations can be initiated with a view to a final settlement.
Second, will the principal adversaries, having agreed to a cease-fire, also agree to have Canada take part in the operation? Here again, Mr. Speaker, the answer is yes.
Third, is this operation likely to serve the cause of peace and to lead to a long-term political settlement? Mr. Speaker, there is no doubt that violent, bitter and costly massacres and battles have ceased, and we hope for good. Furthermore, negotiations between the two countries are to start tomorrow, August 25, in Geneva. We cannot, of course, anticipate the outcome of these negotiations, but we can only hope that the outcome will be positive.
Fourth, we try to find out whether the size and international structure of the Force are appropriate to fulfil the mandate it has been given, and whether our participation in peacekeeping forces will in any way harm Canada's relations with other countries. Having heard what the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Beatty) said on this subject, Mr. Speaker, the House will not doubt that this condition has also been met.
August 24, 1988

Fifth, what we must keep in mind is whether our participation in a particular peacekeeping mission could hurt possible future commitments by Canada. Some of you may be wondering whether we would still be able to fulfil other commitments, given that such a large number of our communications specialists are taking part in this United Nations operation. The answer is yes, Mr. Speaker. Indeed, we have made a very great effort and we also participate in other peacekeeping missions. However, these efforts might limit our ability to accede in the immediate future to a request for peacekeeping forces on the same scale.
Therefore, to meet additional requests, we will have to ensure that United Nations requests for our assistance are as varied as possible. Furthermore, the Government has been careful to make sure that our considerable effort for peace between Iran and Iraq will not prevent us from meeting our other peacetime commitments.
The sixth point that the Government considered before deciding to participate is whether there is an identifiable authority that can support the operation and influence the opponents. In this case, of course, the United Nations is such an authority and it has the support of the Security Council and almost all member countries.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, we must know whether our participation will be adequately and fairly funded and whether the necessary logistic support will be provided. I believe that I can tell the House that the United Nations is seriously attending to this. In addition, Canadian troops will have all the logistic support that my Government is able to provide them.
I believe that I have shown you, Mr. Speaker, that the support given by Members of this House to Canada's participation in this United Nations mission is justified. This participation is based on an objective analysis of the situation and of the results that will likely flow from our efforts.
So, Mr. Speaker, I have no hesitation in supporting the resolution before the House and in urging Hon. Members to do the same without reservation.

Rather than having to deal with conflicts through violence, we can do it through diplomatic means.
