Mr. Speaker, I rise with a great deal of pride as a Canadian, one who has always supported very sincerely the efforts of the Canadian Armed Forces, along with my own Party, in the useful role they play not only nationally but internationally. I think that quite often the image of the Armed Forces is misconstrued. When we talk about the Canadian military community, people have a tendency to think only of getting ready for a war or getting ready for combat of some kind in some part of the world. It is looked upon as having serious rules and regulations that do not always apply in other areas of society. However, that is the reality of any defence community.
Any armed forces must have the solid backing of the Government and the people of the country they serve. They must have strong backing on issues such as the peacekeeping role they are presently playing in Iraq and Iran. That should be in keeping with the role, I would think, of all political Parties in this country and every Canadian citizen.
Through our Armed Forces, we as a nation, are playing an important role in bringing about peace in a war-torn part of the world. Sometimes people ask why we should be involved over there, why not let them go to it? That is an old fashioned way of looking at wars today. Battles going on anywhere in the world must be subdued. Every attempt must be made to keep them under control. Indeed, this battle in Iraq and Iran has not been a small one, particularly in the eyes of the people involved, and it is very important that we do our utmost to bring peace to that war-torn part of the world. By doing so, we will be preventing any spread of that war through accident.
When we review the wars that have started over the years of world history, we can see that many, many accidents have occurred which have been the cause of world wars even though the combatants have been prepared for war. It takes one incident to trigger the whole event.
I would like to say a word about this motion today simply because this is one of many important roles the Canadian Armed Forces have played in peacekeeping around the world. As has already been stated in this debate, peacekeeping on the part of the Canadian Armed Forces was introduced by the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent, and one of its greatest proponents in international affairs was the late Hon. Lester B.
Pearson who became a world renowned diplomat as a Canadian.
I must say something at this time in debate on behalf of the actual participants. I want to say that, living as I do three miles from the Canadian forces base gate at CFB Petawawa, I have a deep sense of pride in the way this whole operation has been put together. A number of dedicated officers formed a committee under a commanding officer and simply started putting certain roles into play. The Minister is in the House today and I am sure he would agree with me that an operation such as this is almost a miniature mobilization plan. A number of people came in from Calgary to join the group. There were approximately 350 personnel to start with at the base at Petawawa. Some 20 personnel came in from the Signals Corps at CFB Kingston. About 40 reserves came in from all across Canada, registered and were assimilated into the force.
There were others from many centres across Canada. In a matter of days these professional people in our Armed Forces put a number of troops together to be sent to a very important task in the Middle East, to observe the lines and the agreement that was laid down by the United Nations and signed by both Iraq and Iran. As observers and communications people on the scene, it is their job to report any infractions of the U.N. mandate as it has been laid down.
That says a great deal for the members of our Armed Forces and our communications role, that they should be chosen to communicate all those messages back to the U.N. and to coordinate the efforts of our Canadian peacekeeping troops as they go ahead in their role, working with other internationals. Only approximately 15 of our own Canadian troops are playing the role as observers. The rest are heavily involved in the communications side. Certainly, in an area of the world where communications are practically non-existent, it is an extremely important role for the Canadian Forces to take over.
When this whole operation was started, the manner in which those vehicles were put through a routine was almost like a major automobile company producing cars. A large number of trucks and jeeps were sent to the Middle East. Those vehicles were taken out of training action. They were put through a long building. In the first room they were screened and made ready for painting. They went into the next room to be painted, and when they came out at the far end of the building they were all painted white with the U.N. sign on them. It was a mass production job, and this was part of it.
Then there is the transportation of these vehicles. This does not only involve sending a number of people off to the Middle East. It involves other people here transporting those vehicles and putting them on to aircraft. In this case, many of the drivers went to the Middle East with the vehicle that they would be driving when they got there. All their papers had to be cleared and in order.
August 24, 1988

I want to say a word or two about publicity. Members of the Armed Forces were seen signing their wills before they left. I believe that that was very crass publicity. It was terrible, and I will tell you why, Mr. Speaker. Quite often when the military community have soldiers leave on military schemes, the CO has the right at any time to ask them if their personal effects are in order. They can check their wills when they leave the country on active duty, and they can check their wills when they go for active duty on peacekeeping. It is a normal routine.
The fact that this was a special move on peacekeeping in the Middle East, that so many media personnel zeroed in on this issue, added to the fear and concern felt by the families of the Armed Forces personnel that those families did not need. The head of the household is going off for a peacekeeping mission for a six-month period and at the end of that period we will see what happens then because it is a very important mission. However, it is important that those families also receive support.
That is another thing that has been put together by the administration on the bases. Mothers who are left at home with families and who do not have a means of going to the grocery store are being looked after. I believe that that story should be told. It is normal procedure for a military community to support its own people. Any questions that are raised in an opportunistic manner about that should be discredited. Those people are not only doing a job for this nation, they are also doing a job for many peoples in the world in their role as peacekeepers.
Many people will talk about the Koreas, Cyprus, and Suez in 1956, which was another very successful venture. There was another operation in the Middle East in 1974 and 1975 when 1,037 peacekeeping troops were in the Middle East. Most of those troops were stationed in Egypt at the time, but many were scattered throughout the Middle East.
In May, 1975, I had the opportunity of travelling to the Middle East. I spent approximately six days with the commanding officer of our Middle East forces. One thing that struck me as we travelled throughout the Middle East at that time was the respect shown to the Canadian forces by people of all nations.
We must remember when members of the Canadian Forces are abroad, they are among the best diplomats that we have in our government service. The Armed Forces are not supposed to be political. However, when members of the Armed Forces go abroad they are totally capable of dealing with nationals on an equal basis, because they learn the system before they go. They are always well briefed. They are also diplomats because they know how to deal with people. They relate to those people. Why? Because they are well briefed on the local situation, and they are well briefed on members of the other nations of the world with whom they will be serving.
As a communications group in the Middle East at the present time, our forces are sending the messages back to the United Nations, back to the national Governments of Iraq and
Peacekeeping
Iran, and back to the commanding officers of the Iraqi and Iranian forces, on behalf of all the military personnel who are serving in the Middle East.
I have mentioned the roles of members of the Canadian Armed Forces politically, diplomatically. Their third role is as professional soldiers. Indeed, they are professional soldiers, and they can play their role well. They can make decisions when decisions have to be made. For this reason they are respected.
I observed our U.N. General go into peacekeeping headquarters in the Middle East. He was totally listened to and totally respected because he knew what he was doing and he knew his business. One morning when we were leaving Beirut at 4.30 a.m. to go to the airport we were stopped in the street by individuals who stuck a sub-machine gun in each car window. The general talked to the individuals, and they backed off and let us through. What a good relationship our troops have with other countries. It was as if nothing had happened; it was just part of their role and part of their duty.
On behalf of our people serving in the Middle East, and certainly on behalf of the people here at home who helped them get to the Middle East and who put this peacekeeping corps together, I want to say that our troops today are playing a traditional role for the Canadian nation that has been going on for several decades.
When we talk about the expenses of peacekeeping, there is one thing about which I am not clear. If the Minister is going to make a closing statement, maybe he could comment on it. I know that when we serviced our own troops in the beginning, we were not given credit for funds spent on the United Nations ledger. It is a good thing that we are serving our own troops in the Middle East because otherwise there would be too much bureaucracy, it would take too long to get the supplies to them, vehicles would be sitting there for weeks or months on end because supplies were not forthcoming as a result of the red tape they have to go through in the United Nations. However, I hope that Canada is receiving full credit in terms of the ledger books of the United Nations for the money spent on maintaining our force while it is there, because I think that is very important. That is really part of our realistic contribution as well.
I think that the key thing that we must all remember on an occasion such as this is that peacekeeping will cost us money. The United Nations will cost us money. But what is the price that the world may pay and that we may pay otherwise? We have been through several major wars in the world, and we know what price we had to pay. Peacekeeping is worth the price. As a nation that is looked upon as a middle power in the world, as one who has many friends all over the world, I do not think that there is a greater tribute that can be paid to our Canadian Armed Forces than for the Parliament of Canada to

August 24, 1988
Peacekeeping
say, "Thank you for your efforts and we wish you well", and to prove to them that we are solidly behind them in their mission.
Last week, I make a statement in this House, commenting on that very thing and saying that we all wish them well as they go about this very important task. Let us start looking at these people as being constructive. Let us look upon our Armed Forces not in the image of war or combat, but as having all the other qualities that they possess and put into practice.
Speaking on behalf of the Liberal Party-and I am sure at this time, remembering the efforts of previous Governments of Louis St. Laurent, Lester B. Pearson and so on-let us remember our forces in the Middle East and wish them every success and Godspeed. We know that they will do a good job on behalf of Canada, on behalf of the United Nations and, indeed, be a tremendous tribute to the world.

That just tells me that if the Minister, instead of sitting in his bathtub playing with model toy nuclear submarines, had spent as much time and attention on transport capacity and reequipping our Armed Forces with the kind of communications expertise that we already have, those kinds of problems would not have occurred in the last few days. I would like to ask the Hon. Member if he would care to comment on that and also on whether or not, as one who walked the green line in Nicosia in 1973, with Greek and Turkish people on each side 20 feet away with fully loaded automatic weapons, the Canadian Forces were fully trusted and respected because we were perceived to be impartial peacekeepers.
It is a role that we can play in a big way. It is not with nuclear submarines. It is the kind of role that Canada can play because of the first-class reputation that we have had. I am
proud of people like Tommy Douglas and Stanley Knowles, who, back in the 1950s and 1960s, supported those kinds of peacekeeping operations that we have been involved in.
It is overwhelming. Canadians have always supported our peacekeeping role. They do now and they will continue to do so. I would like my hon. friend to comment about our capacity in that role and whether or not it has been kept up. I would hope that my hon. friend from Victoria would comment on that as well.

The modern communications system will allow the Canadian Armed Forces to communicate back home. They can communicate with the two Governments in Iraq and Iran. They can communicate with defence headquarters of those two countries. They can get back to the UN. That is why they are there, because they are good at communications and they can do the job.
As far as vehicles are concerned, I do not know whether it has been mentioned in this debate or not, but some of the vehicles that are going to be used could very well come from the Iraqian Armed Forces and some could come from the Iranian Armed Forces, because they were willing to give some of their vehicles over to the peacekeeping troops.
I think that says one solid thing. I would like to point this out to the Hon. Member for Regina East (Mr. Benjamin). These two countries are fed up with war. They had to get out of this war by saving face on both sides.
Canadians, having the qualities that I have just described, are ideal to be sent there, because they have to be seen to be putting the same emphasis on Tehran as they are putting on Baghdad, they are supposed to be seen as putting the same emphasis on Iranian problems as they do on Iraqian problems,and this is part of the diplomatic role. I think that as far as peacekeeping in general is concerned we are not all perfect. I think that we as Canadians should support more transport facilities to assist our Armed Forces in their peacekeeping duties. We should not be too hesitant in accepting help from other nations. After all that helps us out in getting our forces there.

Mr. Speaker, in the few minutes I have available, first let me compliment the Hon. Member for Renfrew-Nipissing-Pembroke (Mr. Hopkins) on his speech. It was in the proper form and stuck to the subject quite well.
As for the Member for whom I have always had a great deal of respect, the Hon. Member for Brant (Mr. Blackburn), the kindest thing I can say about his speech is that it was disappointing. If he feels so keenly that he wants a debate on the White Paper, then I would suggest he speak to the other Member who participated in this debate today and wanted to talk about the White Paper and use one of the opposition days for that purpose. Alternatively, they might have talked their House Leader out of spending five or six days of the time of the House in answering bells he insisted on ringing to ensure that Private Members' Bills which were unanimously supported by the House were voted on.
I would like to bring to the attention of the House Canada's long-standing tradition in peacekeeping. We have been an active and committed member of the United Nations since its inception. We have made an important contribution to world
Peacekeeping
stability by participating in virtually every one of these peacekeeping efforts. It is the manner in which the Canadian Forces have operated that has given Canada a reputation that is worldwide. We have really no competitors when it comes to our very good peacekeeping activities.
Peacekeeping should not be confused with peacemaking, but frequently people do confuse the two. Incidentally, while I enjoyed most of the speech of the Hon. Member for Renfrew-Nipissing-Pembroke, a few remarks about his peacekeeping equipment brought back a memory of the time when I first visited Cyprus, which was 14 years ago. I went on from there to the Sinai Desert where we had another peacekeeping force. The Ghanains were next door to us on the line out in the middle of the Sinai Desert. I noticed that they were better equipped than the Canadian troops of that day, which makes you think that Idi Amin must have been better with his defence budgets than was the Liberal Government of the day.
We are no stranger to intervening between conflicting parties in this peacekeeping role of ours. I would like to mention particularly this one, which I consider to be a more delicate operation than most of the ones in which we have participated. The first thing that must happen about a peacekeeping mission is that both sides must wish to have peace. If one side only wants peace and the other side is still quarrelsome, Canada would run into the danger of being one of the antagonists in the operation, and we cannot afford to do that.
I was very pleased the Minister brought this motion to the House because I have always thought, as many parliamentarians do, that important resolutions such as this should be brought before us as quickly as possible and should always come before Parliament to get the feel of Members as to whether we should or should not participate in certain activities.
I would like to mention one operation in which we took part that was not under the aegis of the United Nations. I am speaking of the time we went into Vietnam in a peacekeeping role in 1973. The then Secretary of State for External Affairs had this to say:
-peace "depends upon the parties to the peace agreement and not upon the International Commission of Control and Supervision. It is only if the parties are co-operating in a strict observance of the agreement-that the Commission can perform its function with any hope of success".
We went in to Vietnam "to supervise a peace, not to umpire a war". The same thing must apply here. We went there for 60 days and then gave another 60 days' warning that we did not like the way things were going and that we might pull out, and we did.
I want to take just one more minute to relate something about the Middle East and why I consider it to be a more delicate situation than most. There is a story that Field Marshall Slim liked to tell about becoming Chief of the General Staff in the days when Britain had an empire of considerable magnitude. When they appointed a new Chief of

the General Staff they claimed there was a book of secret directions to which he should pay attention, a book he would get when he assumed the office. He finally assumed the office and went into the Chiefs office, found the secret box, opened it up and there was a piece of paper with two items on it. It said: "Number One: Never invade Mainland China. Number Two: Never take for granted anything that happens in the Middle East." I trust the Minister will do the same.

Mr. Speaker, certainly we absolutely and unequivocally support the motion that has come forward. I think our defence critic has articulated the reasons.
I want to speak very briefly on the issue of the composition because I believe the Minister for National Defence (Mr. Beatty) in his press conference left the erroneous impression that the decision to bar women and people of Jewish and Arabic background from serving was a directive from the United Nations. In fact, I was in touch through my office with the United Nations and no such directive had been issued. Unfortunately, it seems to be endemic of this Government that when delicate questions like this come up it tends to go ahead without any kind of UN directive. Frankly, there have been occasions in the past when previous Liberal Governments have been asked to send contingents which excluded people on the basis of religious extraction and they refused.
I would suggest that the Minister either listen to the wisdom on this issue from the United Nations and not parade the fact that it was the United Nations that prevented women, Arabs and Jews from participating in this peacekeeping force because that was a decision taken by the Minister directly and by the Government. We feel that, as an over-all strategy, the United Nations may make that decision, but it should not have been made by the Canadian Government. It is typical of the attitude shown toward Captain Woodley. We think discrimination is something that should be addressed. Unfortunately, the Minister lost the opportunity to do so in this particular case.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. I thank the Chair for giving me the opportunity to raise this question and I will be brief because I know it is now six o'clock.
This morning I attended at a panel session of the Canadian Bar Association in Montreal, Quebec. The panel included the Secretary of State (Mr. Bouchard), Barbara Frumm and Michel Roy. There was a discussion on a variety of aspects of politics and the media and the private lives of members of the public.
During the course of that panel discussion this morning, I made references to certain actions of the Hon. Member for Selkirk-Interlake (Mr. Holtmann) during the evening of Wednesday, July 27, and into the wee hours of the morning of Thursday, July 28. I understand that that Member has in fact taken offence to the references that I made to his conduct at that time, and in the circumstances, I certainly wish to take this first opportunity to retract in full and without hesitation the comments that I made with respect to the conduct of that Hon. Member, and further, to apologize to the Hon. Member for the offence he has taken.
